briefing.headline: The simulation predicts the four-day week would cut leavers over the next 12 months by about 43%, from 529 to 297 out of 5,000, with staff feeling clearly positive (+1.11 on a -2 to +2 scale).
briefing.most_at_risk: No group reacts badly; long commuters (-47%) and carers (-46%) gain most because a day saved from commuting or for caring is worth a lot to them, while managers are the most guarded, saying they like it but are 'not going anywhere either way' and doubt the output promise.
risks: The 'same output' condition is the one worry raised in almost every voice: staff fear it quietly means five days of work in four. Vague or heavy-handed measurement could turn goodwill into resentment and burnout among the people already working hardest.

The leaving figure covers 12 months but the trial lasts six. If the policy is withdrawn or watered down after the trial, the retention gain may not last and could reverse, since staff are already asking whether it will stick.

Managers will carry the job of delivering the same output and measuring it, yet they are the most sceptical group. If they are not convinced and equipped, the trial could fail in practice even though staff support it.
design_changes: Define and publish how output will be measured for each team before the trial starts, agree it with the teams, and state plainly that the aim is not to squeeze five days of work into four. Delay the start by a few weeks if that is what it takes to get this right.
Announce up front how the trial will be judged, when the decision will be made, and what happens afterwards, so staff are not left guessing whether the benefit will be taken away.

Brief and support managers first, involve them in setting the output measures, and run short workload and hours check-ins during the trial so you catch overload early rather than at the six-month mark.
briefing.confidence: medium, because the direction (fewer leavers, strong goodwill) is consistent across all 48 voices and every group, but the size of the effect comes from a simulation that shows a near-identical 40-47% drop in every group, so treat 43% as a sign of a strong positive effect rather than a figure to plan headcount on.
